title: Cohere API Trial Key, Rate Limits and Pricing in 2026
summary: Cohere API supports text generation, embeddings, and reranking via HTTPS with a dashboard key. See pricing models, rate limits, and common error responses.
body_markdown:
## Calling the Cohere API from automated workflows


You can make Cohere calls for embedding, classifying or summarising from a workflow builder without running a service, but it adds nothing to Cohere's limits. Your 429s arrive exactly as they would from code, so the same handling applies.


### When to use workflows for Cohere API tasks


Three jobs suit a workflow: embedding each new document as it lands, classifying inbound email, and summarising support tickets, so a single unified approach can handle all three.


Each is event-driven and low volume, and each is a single request with a small amount of glue around it.


A webhook receives the event, a step calls Cohere, and a later step writes the result somewhere. You skip deployment, a process to keep alive and a scheduler to maintain.


Keep the API key in a stored connection rather than in a script, so it stays out of the workflow's own configuration and out of anyone's copy of it.


That matters on a trial key, which you'll want to swap for a production key without editing every step.


Activepieces runs these steps on your own provider key, so the $0.15 per million input tokens for Command R is billed on your Cohere account at Cohere's rate, not at a resold one. MoneyGram, Moneypenny, Alan and FundingSocieties run it in production.


Bring-Your-Own-Key availability is listed tier by tier on the Activepieces pricing page, next to unlimited flows on every plan, free included, so you can set that rate against what a platform charges when it resells its own model and compare the two line by line.


Once sustained throughput is the point, such as bulk re-embedding a whole archive, code is the better tool. There you control concurrency yourself, and a workflow's per-run overhead becomes the bottleneck.


### Retries and pacing against rate limits


Start with the builder's retry setting, the cheapest place to handle failures, and put it on every step that calls Cohere. The screenshot below shows the shape of it using a placeholder action from an ice cream catalogue service, Gelato, rather than Cohere.


Look at the right-hand panel: the selected step carries its connection, a "Continue on Failure" option and an "Auto Retry on Failure" option. Those two switches decide whether a rate-limited call retries or whether the run dies or carries on with an empty result.


Leave "Continue on Failure" off for Cohere steps. A silently skipped classification writes nothing, and you find out from a customer rather than a log.


Automatic retry only repeats a request. It doesn't pace the workflow behind it, so if many events arrive together, queue or space them yourself before they reach the Cohere step.
